questions.stem: Why are glass beads included as a third tube?

options.explanation: Absorbing the gas would hide the result.
Beads cannot respire or catalyse anything.

options.text: To match the volume of the other tubes without adding anything living
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: To feed the seeds during the run
options.explanation: Beads are inert and feed nothing.

questions.stem: Why is the delivery tube's end held just below the limewater surface?

options.explanation: Evaporation is not the concern; contact is.
The test is qualitative cloudiness, not volume.
The seeds sit separately in their own tube.

options.text: So released gas bubbles through the limewater and reacts with it
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: Which alternative indicator turns from orange toward yellow as carbon dioxide accumulates?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Iodine signals starch, not this gas.
Universal indicator tracks pH broadly, not carbon dioxide specifically.
Litmus shows acidity roughly, but the named reagent here is hydrogen-carbonate.

questions.stem: State the volume of limewater poured into each boiling tube.
questions.modelAnswer: Two cubic centimetres of limewater go into the bottom of each tube.

questions.stem: Name the chemical dissolved in limewater.
questions.modelAnswer: Limewater is calcium hydroxide dissolved in water.

questions.stem: Explain why the boiled-seed tube is essential to the carbon dioxide investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: It shows that dead seeds produce no cloudiness, proving the colour change in tube A comes from respiration rather than from the apparatus.

questions.stem: A student finds tube A cloudy but tube B slightly cloudy too. Suggest one cause and one fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Microbes on unsterilised seeds may be respiring in both tubes; sterilising the set-up and using fresh seeds removes the stray source.

questions.stem: Why must the seeds and flasks be sterilised with weak bleach?

options.explanation: Sterilisation has nothing to do with colour.

options.text: So microbes cannot respire and add their own heat to either flask
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Bleach is not a nutrient.
Coat softening is irrelevant to the temperature reading.

questions.stem: Where should each thermometer bulb sit?

options.explanation: The wall warms and cools differently from the seed mass.

options.text: Under the cotton wool seal only
options.explanation: The wool holds the thermometer; the bulb must reach the seeds.

options.text: Among the seeds inside its flask
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: In the room beside the flasks
options.explanation: A room thermometer helps, but the flask reading needs contact with the seeds.

questions.stem: What temperature behaviour is expected in flask A with dead seeds?

options.explanation: Dead seeds do not respire, so no heat is added.
Insulation minimises loss; no sharp fall is expected.
Flask B warms because its seeds are alive.

options.text: Steady, apart from any drift in the room temperature
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: In the recorded results, what change did the germinating-seed flask show?

options.text: A rise of 5.5 degrees Celsius, from 20.0 to 25.5
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Twenty was the starting temperature, not the rise.
Respiration warms; it does not chill.
Living seeds released enough heat to lift the reading clearly.

questions.stem: Why are the flask tops sealed with cotton wool?

options.explanation: Nothing in this set-up absorbs gas.

options.text: It holds the thermometer in place and reduces heat loss
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It lets oxygen flood in freely
options.explanation: The wool is a plug, not an air valve.
Sterilisation is the bleach step, done beforehand.

questions.stem: State the temperature change recorded for the germinating-seed flask.
questions.modelAnswer: It rose by 5.5 degrees Celsius, from 20.0 to 25.5.

questions.stem: Name the solution used to sterilise the seeds and flasks.
questions.modelAnswer: A weak bleach solution sterilises them before the run.

questions.stem: Explain why a temperature rise in flask A would point to the room, not the seeds.
questions.modelAnswer: Because dead seeds cannot respire, any warming there must come from the surroundings, which is why room temperature is monitored alongside.

questions.stem: Both flasks drift up by 1 degree, but flask B climbs 5.5 in total. Interpret the numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: The shared 1-degree drift reflects the room; the extra 4.5 degrees in flask B is the heat released by its respiring seeds.

questions.stem: In the carbon dioxide set-up, when is the limewater observed?

options.explanation: Days suit the heat-flask run, not this one.
Gas needs time to accumulate and react.

options.text: After about three hours in the warm environment
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The named window is about three hours.

questions.stem: What does the letter S in CORMS stand for?

options.explanation: S is about constancy, not selection.
Sterilisation belongs to the method, not the CORMS letter.
No letter tracks ordering.

options.text: Same — the factors held constant across tubes
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Which factor belongs in the Change slot for the limewater investigation?

options.text: The tube contents: germinating seeds, dead seeds or beads
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Temperature is held constant, so it belongs in the Same list.
Volume is controlled, not varied.
Nothing about the observer changes between tubes.

questions.stem: Why repeat each investigation several times?

options.explanation: Small variation is expected; repeats expose it.

options.text: For reliability: one anomalous run should not drive the conclusion
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Repeats answer reliability, not logistics.
Repeats do not warm anything.

questions.stem: Which measurement settles the heat claim, and after how long?

options.explanation: That belongs to the limewater set-up.
Mass is not recorded in this practical.

options.text: Thermometer temperature, initially and again after 2-3 days
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: State the CORMS letters in order.
State one factor kept the same across the three limewater tubes.
questions.modelAnswer: The volume of indicator is the same in every tube.

questions.stem: Explain why the glass-bead tube strengthens the limewater conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer: Because beads occupy volume like seeds but never respire, so a clear tube C rules out the apparatus itself as the source of the cloudiness.

questions.stem: Draft the CORMS Change and Measurement entries for testing blowfly larvae instead of seeds.
questions.modelAnswer: Change the tube contents to larvae against an empty control, and observe the limewater cloudiness after the same three-hour window.
